How dirty are you cops?” a handcuffed Whiteway shouted. The officers didn’t audibly react to Whiteway’s comments, but a couple of soft claps could be heard as Justice Mark Poland found him guilty of both charges he was facing, attempted murder and aggravated assault, and again after the judge dismissed a pair of charter challenges the defence had raised in hopes of having the charges stayed . Whiteway, 37, who was denied bail and has been behind bars for two years, is expected to be sentenced early next year. Article content Ryan Whiteway appears in a Sarnia courtroom by video link from the Sarnia Jail shortly after his arrest in August 2024. Whiteway was convicted Tuesday of attempted murder and aggravated assault in the stabbing of a Sarnia police constable in a downtown condo building on Aug. 20, 2024. (Charles Vincent/Special to Postmedia Network) ‘EMOTIONAL’ REACTION TO VERDICT Brown, after exchanging hugs with several co-workers in the lobby, declined to comment on the outcome. His parents, Fred and Kathy, didn’t want to speak on his behalf, but observed this has weighed heavily on him. “It’s been tough,” Fred Brown said. “It’s a lot of weight off. Emotional,” said a choked-up Reg Musclow, a Sarnia police detective and close friend of Brown’s. Article content Deputy Chief Mike Van Sickle said he was happy for Brown and called the trial part of the healing process. “Although the physical injuries heal, the traumatic effect of an incident like this will last – it could be forever, right? So it’s good that this part is done and the healing can continue,” he said. Detective constables Karl Brown, left, and Erik Ostenfeldt with Sarnia police are shown at the Ontario Medal for Police Bravery ceremony in 2025. Handout ‘HARD FOR HIM TO HEAR’ Whiteway’s lawyer, Nicole DeBellefeuille, said her client maintains what he testified at trial: he thought someone broke into his condo, he didn’t know it was the police, and he wasn’t trying to kill anyone. “It was hard for him to hear that everything he said was rejected,” she said of the judge’s findings. DeBellefeuille said she expected they’d be at the Appeal Court on the issue. She also said she was “particularly shocked” about the findings on their charter challenge and the police’s use of force. THE STABBING AT THE SEAWAY CENTRE On Aug. 20, 2024, Brown, then a 37-year-old Sarnia police constable, was attacked while checking on Whiteway’s well-being inside his 15th-floor Seaway Centre condo. He needed 100 stitches, four blood transfusions and surgery on his thumb. Whiteway, 37, was arrested that night and charged with attempted murder and aggravated assault. Article content At trial, Whiteway testified he thought the officers were aliens there to abduct him. He said he was a paranoid hermit who used drugs such as crystal meth, hash, THC and shatter. When the bathroom door flew open amid the well-being check and a ray of light – Brown’s flashlight – was shone on him, he reached for a self-defence tool, a collector’s knife, and attacked the “entity.” Whiteway was found fit to stand trial after a criminal responsibility assessment , which was ordered in late 2024. While testifying, he also denied wanting to kill Brown and said had he known it was law enforcement, he would have acted differently. He also alleged he was assaulted by three or four Sarnia police officers for five or 10 minutes in what he called a brutal beat-down after his arrest, and again in the back of a cruiser. A Sarnia police cruiser is parked outside the Seaway Centre in Sarnia on Aug. 21, 2024, the day after Sarnia police said one of their officers was stabbed multiple times in the head and neck during a welfare check. (Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer) CLOSING AND STAY ARGUMENTS DeBellefeuille argued for a stay of the charges due to the alleged police assault. She also argued police had no right to enter her client’s unit and that he acted in self-defence. Prosecutor Nila Mulpuru countered there was no evidence multiple officers assaulted Whiteway and the evidence they did have didn’t support self-defence. She also pointed to exigent circumstances, which allows for searches without warrants to prevent imminent bodily harm. Article content POLAND’S DECISION Poland, who heard the case over five days this summer without a jury, spent more than an hour Tuesday explaining his decisions to convict Whiteway and dismiss the charter challenges. He said this case was about why Whiteway stabbed Brown and what he intended, along with examining the assertion that police had used excessive force. He broke it down into four main issues: ISSUE #1: LAWFUL AUTHORITY TO ENTER Poland found the police did not breach Whiteway’s charter rights by entering his condo without prior authorization. He explained the Crown had to prove on a balance of probabilities their entry was authorized by law and reasonable. In the end, he found their decision to enter Whiteway’s home was justified. He pointed out Whiteway was well-known to police and officers had attended three times by the time Brown and Erik Ostenfeldt, his partner for the well-being check, arrived. They also met with a well-placed source, a neighbour who called police concerned for Whiteway’s well-being after they heard painful, distressed screaming that suddenly stopped, before going to Whiteway’s unit. Poland said the officers waiting about 17 minutes for the master key from a staff member did not diminish the exigent circumstances. And after going inside, he found they did what was expected of them by going into the locked bathroom amid their concerns for his well-being. Article content The judge also said police conduct must be assessed in the circumstances as they appeared at the time, not in hindsight. ISSUE #2: SELF-DEFENCE Poland said it was up to the Crown to neutralize the defence’s self-defence argument – and it did. He pointed to part of the law that says the act committed must be reasonable in the circumstances. Poland said it wasn’t reasonable for Whiteway to stab Brown if he knew Brown was a police officer. The judge found Whiteway did know this, despite his repeated denials. Police had been at his door 22 times in the past, according to Whiteway’s own testimony, and he also recorded a video through the peephole that night, which shows Brown and Ostenfeldt wearing their uniforms. Whiteway can be heard saying, “Yeah, head out, boy,” after the staffer gives them the master key and, “It’s going to get rough in here, boy,” shortly before they enter. Poland said he found Whiteway was aware police were there and intended to enter and the video demonstrated he didn’t adopt a panic room mode in response to unknown attendants, as he had testified. An email Whiteway sent shortly before the clash also was important in ascertaining his state of knowledge as it included the phrase “unauthorized entry,” which points to his knowing it was police, Poland said. Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer/Postmedia Network Photo by Terry Bridge / Terry Bridge/The Observer ISSUE #3: INTENT TO MURDER The Crown also had to prove the specific intent to murder beyond a reasonable doubt, Poland explained. Once again, it did. The judge rejected Whiteway’s testimony that he just attacked at the light. He pointed out the majority of the blows were inflicted on the vital and exposed parts of Brown’s body, such as his head and neck. He also used army-style knives and the element of surprise and stabbed from a position of tactical advantage. After reviewing all the evidence, Poland said he was left without reasonable doubt Whiteway intended to murder Brown and convicted him. “I’m not going back to school for police foundations,” Whiteway uttered from the prisoner’s box in response. ISSUE #4: CRUEL AND UNUSUAL PUNISHMENT As for the cruel and unusual punishment charter argument, Poland said after rejecting Whiteway’s testimony he was left with no evidence that happened. Photos of damaged drywall with blood stains in his unit were not sufficient on their own. Poland noted Ostenfeldt had Brown’s blood mainly on the back of his uniform and there could have been incidental blood transfer on the wall. All of the officers denied assaulting Whiteway and the judge rejected Whiteway’s assertion he was beaten by three to four officers over five to 10 minutes. Josh Mitchell testified a handcuffed Whiteway resisted arrest while he was briefly in a one-in-one situation with him and he had to turn custody over to other officers, worrying he would lose control after seeing his close friend, Brown, hurt and possibly dying. But Mitchell said he did not recall punching Whiteway or damaging the drywall. Poland noted Whiteway did not link any of the damage to the one-on-one encounter with Mitchell, just to an alleged group beat-down, which the judge said clearly did not occur. The judge did say he found it unusual Mitchell was the only officer who said Whiteway resisted and that he directed the other officers out of the unit and was left alone with him. He added he had significant concerns about Mitchell’s reliability and credibility, raising questions about the precise nature of the application of force that did occur. But, with Whiteway’s credibility and reliability sorely imperiled, he was left with no evidence that Whiteway was assaulted. Whiteway also failed to point out any physical characteristics of the officer who allegedly punched him in the back of the cruiser, despite being in close proximity, the judge said. ‘WELL-ARTICULATED’ JUDGEMENT Van Sickle called Poland’s decision a well-articulated, well-researched and methodical evaluation of the evidence. “So I was very appreciative of that,” the deputy chief said. As for the assault allegations against their officers, Musclow said DeBellefeuille is a tenacious, very good defence lawyer who went over everything with a fine-tooth comb. “As you saw in the verdict from the judge, they were unfounded,” Musclow added. https://www.planetf1.com/news/max-versta.text: Verstappen's extension is a big boost to Red Bull said Mekies. Laurent Mekies said Max Verstappen ’s decision to stay at Red Bull was because of the work of 2,000 people behind the scenes. Red Bull’s drop in performance, coupled with Verstappen’s unhappiness with the current regulations, had plenty predicting that he could leave for another team, or quit the sport entirely. Verstappen extension explained by Red Bull boss He put an end to those rumours in the build-up to the Dutch Grand Prix, announcing he would not only continue with Red Bull next season, but that he had signed on for a further two seasons until 2030. Verstappen’s existing deal was until 2028, but a well-publicised exit clause meant he could have decided after the Hungarian Grand Prix to leave the team. That clause was based on Verstappen’s position in the Drivers’ standings, with the driver permitted to end his stay if he was outside of the top two as Formula 1 entered its summer break after Hungary. But despite being sixth in the standings, and still chasing a first Grand Prix win for F1 2026, Verstappen affirmed his commitment to Red Bull. Team principal Mekies has said it has brought “massive stability” to Red Bull. “It’s massively important,” he said of Verstappen’s extension. “You know the good guys, and in the end of the day, you are only interested in the good guys and girls. “The good guys, they have the choice and I’m talking about our people, and I’m talking about the people in other teams. They have the choice because they are very, very good at what they do. They have the choice. “And as much as Max had to choose which team to commit to, they have the choice to commit left or right and we are all united by only one thing: we want to win. “And when you’re able to say that the fastest driver in the world is with us, it’s a massive stability element. It’s a massive ambition element. “Then everybody understands that everything else that you are being that you are set up is only with that single objective history. So it’s a very big element. More on Max Verstappen from PlanetF1.com PF1 verdict: Max Verstappen has committed to Red Bull, rightly or wrongly Max Verstappen makes escape clause confession in new Red Bull contract “We must not use that as an excuse. So it’s a very big plus. We need to work on everything else to make sure that we keep developing and attracting all the talents.” Mekies was asked by PlanetF1.com if this was the defining moment of his Red Bull tenure but suggested it was not his personal achievement and made note to highlight the unknown names of those working at the factory. “Honestly, nothing to do with leadership moments or whatsoever,” he said. “It’s a teamwork. It’s a huge teamwork. It’s 2,000 people working, and it’s about trying to lay down the facts that will convince Max that we are able to produce the best package in the future, and that his inputs are well used in order for us to produce that best package. “That’s what the group is working day and night on, too. We are we are not going to change our approach. We are still going to be extremely brutally honest with each other. “So we are still going to complain when the car is not fast enough. We are still going to express frustrations when we feel we could have extracted more, or when we feel we are not progressing fast enough. “That’s what drives us out of the bed every day, and we aren’t going to change that. But it’s something that fires every single person in Milton Keynes. It’s something that fires Max every day, and that’s what you like as well.” Additional reporting by Thomas Maher Want to be the first to know exclusive information from the F1 paddock?
